title: Direct and inverse proportion
summary: Recognise direct and inverse proportion, determine the constant of proportionality, and solve contextual problems using equations, tables and checks.
objectives: Distinguish direct proportion from inverse proportion using invariant quantities.
Find and use a constant of proportionality from data or context.
Form equations and test whether answers fit the stated relationship.

blocks.text: Two variables are in direct proportion when multiplying one by a factor multiplies the other by the same factor. Their quotient y/x remains constant. They are in inverse proportion when multiplying one by a factor divides the other by that factor, so their product xy remains constant.

Do not decide from one pair of values alone. Test several rows of a table or use the relationship described by the context. A quantity that increases when another increases is not automatically directly proportional: y = 3x + 5 increases with x but is not direct proportion because y/x changes and its graph does not pass through the origin.

sections.title: Model direct proportion with y = kx

blocks.text: For direct proportion, divide a known y-value by its matching x-value to find k. The constant k is the amount of y for one unit of x, so include its meaning and unit when the variables describe real quantities. Substitute k into y = kx before using a new value.

A direct-proportion table has a constant y/x in every valid row, and its graph is a straight line through the origin. The point (0, 0) matters: if zero items still carry a fixed fee, the total cost is linear but is not directly proportional to the number of items.
In the first diagram, y = 2x: from (2, 4) to (4, 8), x doubles and y doubles, and the straight line passes through the origin.

sections.title: Worked example: direct proportion

prompt.text: The mass m grams of identical metal rods is directly proportional to their total length L centimetres. A total length of 75 cm has mass 210 g. Find the mass of 130 cm of the same rod.

content.text: Write the direct-proportion model and find k.
State the answer with the requested unit: the mass is 364 g.

sections.verification_note: The new length is 130/75 times the old length, and 364/210 = 130/75, so both quantities changed by the same factor.

sections.title: Model inverse proportion with xy = k

blocks.text: For inverse proportion, multiply a known pair to find k. Common contexts include a fixed job shared among equally productive workers, travel time for a fixed distance at different constant speeds, or the dimensions of a rectangle with fixed area. The assumptions must remain valid: adding workers helps only if they work at the same rate and can share the task without interference.

An inverse-proportion graph is a decreasing curve in the positive quadrant for positive quantities. It approaches the axes but never reaches them, because x = 0 would require division by zero. In a table, x doubling makes y halve; x multiplying by five makes y one fifth as large.

In the second diagram, xy = 12: from (2, 6) to (4, 3), x doubles and y halves. Sometimes a quantity depends on two others at once. For a job, the worker-days needed are directly proportional to the size of the job, while for a fixed job the number of days is inversely proportional to the number of workers; this combination is called joint proportion.

sections.title: Worked example: inverse proportion

prompt.text: Nine pumps with equal output can empty a reservoir in 16 hours. Assuming they work continuously at the same rate, how long would 12 pumps take?

content.text: For a fixed job, the number of pumps and the time are inversely proportional.
Use 12 pumps and solve for the time.

sections.verification_note: The number of pumps increased by a factor of 12/9 = 4/3, and the time decreased by the reciprocal factor: 16 × 3/4 = 12 hours.

sections.title: Worked example: a team changes part-way through

prompt.text: A job needs 16 equally productive workers for 9 days. After 3 days, 4 workers leave. How many more days do the remaining workers need to finish the job?

content.text: Measure the whole job in worker-days.
Work out how much is done in the first 3 days and how much is left.
Twelve workers remain, so divide the remaining work by 12.

sections.verification_note: Check the total: 16 × 3 + 12 × 8 = 48 + 96 = 144 worker-days, the whole job. The job takes 3 + 8 = 11 days, longer than 9, as expected when workers leave.

sections.title: Translate the context and reject false models

blocks.text: Name the variables, state the proportional relationship and find k from a matching pair. Keep pairs aligned when reading a table. After solving, describe how the variables should move: direct proportion keeps their change factors equal, while inverse proportion keeps the factors reciprocal.

Some situations only approximate a proportional model. A journey may include fixed stopping time; a group task may not divide perfectly; a price may include a delivery charge. Use direct or inverse proportion only when the question states it or when the assumptions justify a constant quotient or product. Check units and reject impossible results such as negative workers or a time longer after adding equally productive workers to the same divisible job.

prompt.text: A fixed job takes 12 workers 15 days. Assuming inverse proportion and equal productivity, enter the number of days needed by 20 workers.

feedback.text: Worker-days stay constant: 12 × 15 = 180, then 180 ÷ 20 = 9 days. More workers give a shorter time, which fits inverse proportion.

blocks.text: For direct proportion, test that y/x is constant, write y = kx and expect both quantities to change by the same factor. Its graph is a straight line through the origin.

For inverse proportion, test that xy is constant, write y = k/x and expect reciprocal change factors. State the assumptions, use matching data pairs, preserve units and check the direction of change before accepting the answer.
